rotation.topic: Bypassing Safety Controls · Stop Work Authority

openingMessage: Winning is fun, but winning is not the point. Wanting to win is the point. Not giving up is the point. Never letting up is the point.
openingWhy: A long clean streak is exactly when crews get bit — because a good record starts feeling like PPE. It isn't. Last quarter's zero doesn't test today's atmosphere. Never letting up IS the safety program.
leadershipThought: Recognition is culture in action. When you name what someone did right, you tell the whole crew what right looks like. Kudos to the ones doing it right every day.

specialFocus.title: Open the Box Before You Roll — Benzene Monitor In, Shown, Then Go
specialFocus.why: Simple one this morning, and it's thirty seconds well spent. Every air job runs with a benzene monitor — it's the control standing between our crew and an exposure you can't always smell coming. The bad day goes like this: sixty miles out, rigged up, you open the benzene box and it's empty. The monitor is on the charger back at the yard, or riding in somebody else's truck. Now the job waits on us — or worse, somebody gets tempted to start without it. And that is Jacob's topic this week exactly: showing up without the control is bypassing it before the job even begins. The fix is small and it happens in the yard, not on location: open the box, eyes on the monitor, turn it on, show your lead, then roll. Simple steps, every morning, so we get to the job site with the tools we need.
specialFocus.standardLabel: The Yard Check — Thirty Seconds Before the Truck Moves
standard: Open the benzene box every morning — don't trust the weight of it or yesterday's memory. Lid up, eyes on the monitor, inside the box, before it goes in the truck. 'It was in there yesterday' is not a check.

Turn it on in the yard: charged, no faults, bump and calibration current. A monitor that won't power up at the wellhead is the same as no monitor at all — find that out at the yard, where it's a two-minute fix.

Show your lead before you leave. Lid open, monitor on, a quick nod — that's the whole thing. Two sets of eyes on purpose. Leads: be at the line when the trucks pull out and make it easy — a ten-second look, not a ceremony.

Work together. Partners check each other's boxes and the rest of the kit with it: 4-gas, SCBA and work packs, mask bags, JSA paperwork, location sign. One man reads it off, the other man touches each item. Missing anything? The truck doesn't roll — call your lead and we find it before we drive, not after.

Coming home counts too. Monitor back in the box and on the charger, any fault tagged and told to your lead that night — so tomorrow's crew never opens an empty box. Leave the box ready for the next man the way you'd want to find it.

The photo proves TODAY. The monitor picture on your form gets taken fresh — on that location, that day. Last week's reviews caught monitor photos stamped from other days, one from years back. A recycled picture tells a client we were somewhere else; a fresh one is proof the control was really there.

scenarios.title: Sixty Miles and an Empty Box
scenarios.body: Early start, long drive, the crew's rigged up and the company man is ready. The tech pops the benzene box — empty. The monitor's on the charger at the yard where it got left last night. Now there's a phone call, a two-hour round trip or a borrowed monitor nobody's checked, a customer waiting on Canon, and a job that can't start. And the quiet temptation: 'it's a short job, readings have been zero all week.' That's the bypass — and it's never the answer. Rewind to 5:45 AM at the yard: lid up, monitor in, power on, the lead sees it. Thirty seconds and the whole bad morning never happens. Who in the circle has opened an empty box on location — what did it cost?

questions: Walk us through your yard check out loud — what do you open, what do you turn on, and who sees it before you leave?
What else in your truck are you trusting is there without looking? Name one item you'll start touching every morning.
Leads: what makes the 'show me before you go' easy for your crew instead of a hassle?
Today's send-off: no truck leaves this yard until its benzene box has been opened in front of a lead. Who's first?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: No truck leaves the yard until the benzene box is open, the monitor is in it and on, and a lead has seen it. Simple steps, every morning — we get to the job with the tools we need, and the control is on location before the job starts.
